lines.text: Do you know how a pressure cooker cooks so fast? It cheats the boiling point of water.
In a normal pot, water can't get hotter than a hundred degrees. Once it boils, the extra heat just turns it into steam.
A pressure cooker locks its lid. The steam can't escape, so the pressure inside builds up.
Under that pressure, water has to get hotter before it boils, up to about a hundred and twenty degrees.
Hotter water cooks food much faster. Beans that take hours in a pot can be done in under an hour.
A valve on the lid lets steam out if the pressure gets too high. That's the hiss you hear.
The idea goes back to 1679, when a French scientist, Denis Papin, built a steam digester.
So a pressure cooker turns up the heat, just by trapping the steam.
